column5: Comput. Linguist.
column6: Similarity of Semantic Relations
column7:
RQ1: Analogy Generation Method
The paper introduces Latent Relational Analysis (LRA), a method for measuring relational similarity between word pairs. LRA extends the Vector Space Model (VSM) approach in three key ways:

Pattern generation: LRA automatically discovers patterns from a corpus rather than using a fixed set of patterns
Synonym exploration: It uses a thesaurus to find variations of word pairs to handle sparse data
Dimensionality reduction: It applies Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to smooth frequency data

LRA works by representing the relationship between a word pair (e.g., "mason:stone") as a vector where elements correspond to pattern frequencies in a corpus. These patterns capture the contexts in which the word pairs appear together.
column8:
LRA was evaluated on two main tasks:

SAT analogy questions: 374 multiple-choice questions from college entrance exams, where the system must identify which of five word pairs has the most similar relation to a given stem pair.
Noun-modifier classification: 600 noun-modifier pairs labeled with 30 semantic relations (later grouped into 5 broader classes), using nearest neighbor classification with LRA as the similarity measure.
column9:
Strengths:

Performs at human-level on SAT analogy questions (56.1% accuracy vs 57% for average college-bound students)
Significantly outperforms previous approaches (VSM achieved 47.1%)
Handles sparse data by using synonyms to explore variations of word pairs
Automatically discovers patterns rather than relying on manually created patterns
Uses SVD to reduce noise and address sparseness in the data

Weaknesses:

Computationally expensive (took 9 days to process 374 SAT questions)
Requires significant computing resources
Semantic content is distributed across many elements in the vector, making it difficult to interpret why a particular analogy was selected
column10:
Strengths:

SAT analogy questions provide a standardized benchmark with human performance metrics
The evaluation covers a diverse range of semantic relations
Using both SAT questions and noun-modifier classification demonstrates generality
Ablation studies clearly show the contribution of each component

Weaknesses:

Limited datasets (374 SAT questions, 600 noun-modifier pairs)
Noun-modifier dataset has small sample sizes for each relation class (average of 20 examples per class)
The choice of classification scheme for semantic relations may not be optimal
column11:
The paper identifies several challenges in analogy generation:

Handling sparse data: Many word pairs don't co-occur frequently in the corpus
Computational complexity: Processing large matrices requires significant resources
Pattern selection: Identifying meaningful patterns among millions of possibilities
Interpreting vectors: The meaning is distributed across many dimensions, making it difficult to explain why one analogy is better than another
Distinguishing near vs. far analogies: Some analogies involve pairs with high attributional similarity while others don't
column12:
The paper discusses several challenges in evaluating analogical reasoning:

Limited datasets: More extensive labeled data would enable better assessment
Classification scheme subjectivity: Different semantic relation classification schemes exist
Human-level performance: Determining appropriate benchmarks for comparison
Balance between precision and recall: Different applications have different requirements
Computational efficiency: Evaluating computationally intensive methods thoroughly requires substantial resources

column5: Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on World Wide Web
column6: Measuring the similarity between implicit semantic relations from the web
column7:
This paper introduces a method for measuring similarity between implicit semantic relations in two word pairs (relational similarity) using web search. The method consists of three main components:

Lexical Pattern Extraction: Given two word pairs (a,b) and (c,d), the system extracts patterns that represent the semantic relations between words in each pair by:
Retrieving snippets from web search results where the two words co-occur
Replacing the original words with variables (X and Y)
Generating subsequences from the snippets following specific constraints
Counting pattern frequencies across word pairs


Pattern Clustering: The system identifies patterns that express the same semantic relation by:
Using a sequential clustering algorithm that compares pattern distributions across word pairs
Grouping patterns with similar distributions into clusters
Creating feature vectors for word pairs based on these clusters


Mahalanobis Distance Learning: The system measures relational similarity by:
Learning a Mahalanobis distance metric from examples of relationally similar and dissimilar word pairs
Computing the similarity between two word pairs as the Mahalanobis distance between their feature vectors



As the authors explain: "Given two word pairs, (a,b) and (c,d), we design a function, relsim((a, b),(c, d)), that returns a similarity score in the range [0, 1]. The proposed relational similarity measure first extracts implicitly stated relations that exist between the two words in each word pair. The measure then compares the extracted relations between word pairs."
column8:
The method was evaluated using two key tasks:

Relation Classification Task (ENT dataset):

Created a dataset with 100 instances of 5 relation types (20 instances each)
Relations include: ACQUIRER-ACQUIREE, PERSON-BIRTHPLACE, CEO-COMPANY, COMPANY-HEADQUARTERS, and PERSON-FIELD
Used 5-fold cross-validation
Measured classification accuracy and average precision
Compared against baseline methods: Vector Space Model (VSM), Latent Relational Analysis (LRA), and Euclidean distance (EUC)


SAT Word Analogy Questions:

Used 374 questions from the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT)
Each question contains a stem word pair and five choice word pairs
System selects the choice word pair with highest relational similarity to the stem
Measured performance by percentage of correctly answered questions
Compared against 15 other algorithms
column9:
Strengths:

Efficiency: "The proposed method requires only two search engine queries to compute the relational similarity between two word pairs." This significantly reduces processing time compared to LRA, which "takes over 9 days to answer the 374 SAT analogy questions" versus "less than 6 hours" for the proposed method.
No external resources: "The proposed method requires no external resources such as synonym dictionaries to compute relational similarity." This is particularly important for named entities that are "not well covered by manually created dictionaries such as WordNet."
Language independence: The pattern extraction algorithm "requires no language dependent preprocessing steps such as part-of-speech tagging or dependency parsing, which can be time consuming or even infeasible at the Web scale."
Inter-cluster correlation: The method accounts for correlations between different semantic relations by learning a Mahalanobis distance metric, unlike methods that "assume semantic relations to be independent."

Weaknesses:

Performance on certain relations: The method performs relatively poorly on some relation types, particularly "person-birthplace" where analysis revealed "many snippets that convey information related to places that people associate with places other than their place of birth."
SAT performance: While efficient, the method still achieves lower accuracy (51.1%) on SAT questions than the state-of-the-art LRA (56.1%), though LRA uses synonym dictionaries that are unavailable for named entities.
Dynamic nature of relations: The paper acknowledges that "relational similarity is a dynamic phenomenon: it varies with time" which poses a challenge for any method.
Multiple relations: "There can be more than one relation between a given word pair," requiring the system to extract all possible relations.
column10:
Strengths:

Real-world applications: The evaluation tasks (relation classification and SAT questions) represent practical applications of relational similarity.
Comparison to human performance: The SAT evaluation provides a direct comparison to human performance (57% for high school students).
Multiple metrics: The relation classification task is evaluated using both accuracy and average precision, which "integrates the precision at different ranks."
Comparative analysis: The method is compared against multiple baselines, including the state-of-the-art LRA.

Weaknesses:

Limited relation types: The ENT dataset covers only five relation types, which may not represent the full diversity of semantic relations.
Dataset size: The ENT dataset contains only 100 instances (20 per relation), which is relatively small.
Artificial tasks: SAT analogy questions are somewhat artificial and may not represent how relational similarity is used in real-world contexts.
Self-created dataset: The ENT dataset was created by the authors themselves rather than being a standard benchmark dataset.
column11:
The paper identifies several challenges in generating and measuring relational similarity:

Temporal dynamics: "Relational similarity is a dynamic phenomenon: it varies with time. For example, two companies can be competitors initially; subsequently one company might acquire the other."
Multiple relations: "There can be more than one relation between a given word pair. For example, between the two words ostrich and bird, aside from the relation is a large, there is also the relation is a flightless."
Expression variability: "There can be more than one way to express a particular semantic relation in a text. For example, the three patterns – X was acquired by Y, Y completed the acquisition of X, and Y buys X – all indicate an acquisition relation between X and Y."
Named entities: "Measuring relational similarity between pairs in which one or both words are named entities (e.g., company names, personal names, locations, etc.) is even more difficult because such words are not well covered by manually created dictionaries such as WordNet."
Computational complexity: The efficiency challenges of previous methods like LRA, which requires "numerous search engine queries" and "takes over 9 days to process the 374 SAT analogy questions."
column12:
The paper also highlights several challenges in evaluating relational similarity measures:

Lack of benchmarks: The authors had to create their own ENT dataset for evaluating relational similarity between named entities because existing benchmarks were limited.
Query limitations: "Methods that require numerous queries impose a heavy load on search engines" making evaluation difficult at scale.
Resource availability: "In the case of named entities, thesauri of related words are not usually available or are not complete," limiting the application of some methods (like LRA) that rely on such resources.
Multiple expressions: The same semantic relation can be expressed using different lexical patterns, making it difficult to determine when two different-looking relations are actually the same.
Result interpretation: "The classification accuracy does not evaluate the relative rankings of similarity scores," necessitating additional metrics like average precision.

column6: {P}arallel{PARC}: A Scalable Pipeline for Generating Natural-Language Analogies
column7:
"We employed GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003)1 (Brown et al., 2020) (see implementation details in Appendix A.2). We first naïvely tried to ask GPT repetitively for two analogous scientific processes data. We found that GPT (1) tends to repeat itself, and (2) often creates analogies revolving around extremely similar topics." 
"we developed two separate prompts, one for finding an analogous subject and identify similar relations, and another for taking the subject and relations and turning them into paragraphs in natural language"

Process Steps:
Candidate generation using GPT-3.5:
“We employed GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003)... For each paragraph in ProPara, we generate 3 analogy candidates in 4 broad domains, resulting in 4680 samples.”
Human annotation on a subset:
“We hired Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers... The task is to determine whether the paragraphs are analogous and the similar relations are correct.”
Auto-labeling using GPT-4 based on few-shot examples from human annotations:
“We decided to use part of our annotated data as few-shot examples for our filtering model… we use GPT-4.”
Distractor generation (challenging negatives) with GPT-4:
“We use GPT-4 to automatically generate distractors… by switching the order of events.”
column8:
Human annotations: "Workers received two paragraphs, base B and target T , corresponding subjects, domains, and the similar relations generated by the LLM. The task is to determine whether the paragraphs are analogous and the similar relations are correct. If they are, the worker needs to select between close analogy (close topic, similar entities) or far analogy (unrelated topics). If there is an issue with the analogy or the relations, the worker marks it “for further inspection”, along with a reason: dissimilar relations, misinformation, cyclic vs. non-cyclic process, or other (with a free-text explanation)."
"Note that two processes may be deemed analogous or not depending on the annotator’s abstraction, which is affected by their domain knowledge. To ameliorate this, we explicitly instructed annotators to focus on relational similarity, between relations as they are expressed in the texts, and not take domain knowledge into account."

Automatic Evaluation:
Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore
Used to compare generated analogies against human-written references for n-gram and embedding-level similarity.

Two-stage crowd-sourced annotation:
Stage 1: Workers filter out low-quality outputs.
Stage 2: Remaining analogies are rated on three dimensions:
Grammaticality/Coherence/Analogicality
Rating is on a Likert scale from 1 to 5.

Evaluation Method:
Binary classification & multiple-choice tasks on the ProPara-Logy benchmark:
“We propose binary classification and multiple-choice tasks. We evaluate the performance of both humans and state-of-the-art models…”
Human validation of gold-set:
“We show annotators both the most likely analogous candidates, as predicted by the model, but also the least likely candidates.”
Model benchmarking:
“We tested ChatGPT3, GPT-4... FlanT5-small, FlanT5-XL, and FlanT5-XXL... with their official implementations and default parameters.”
column9:

“Our pipeline is easy to adapt to new domains, requiring only small changes in the prompts.”

Diversity & complexity:
“We believe they [relations] can also serve as potential explanations, highlighting the structural similarity between base and target paragraphs.”

Weaknesses:

column5: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
column6: {ANALOGYKB}: Unlocking Analogical Reasoning of Language Models with A Million-scale Knowledge Base
column7:
Step 1: Source Data Collection
“We choose the two most-used KGs, i.e., ConceptNet and Wikidata... we randomly sample 5 million concepts with 813 relations from Wikidata, resulting in 20 million concept pairs.” (p. 6)

Step 2: Acquiring Analogies of the Same Relation
“We can directly utilize the concept pairs in the KGs to generate analogies of the same relations.” (p. 6)

Step 3: Acquiring Analogies of Analogous Relations
Used InstructGPT003 to select analogous relation pairs (e.g., “CEO” ↔ “head of state”) based on semantic similarity.

Two filtering rules were applied:
Symmetry check: If R1 is analogous to R2, then R2 should also be analogous to R1.
Meta-relation induction: Relations must share an abstract meta-relation like "created by" or "head of organization".

Final results were manually reviewed for quality:
“We adopt a third filtering by recruiting two volunteers to manually examine the remaining results…” (p. 8)
column8:
Evaluation Methods:
Automatic Accuracy Check:

“We adopt six analogy benchmarks, i.e., E-KAR (Chen et al., 2022), BATS (Gladkova et al., 2016), UNIT 2 and UNIT 4 (Boteanu and Chernova, 2015), Google (Mikolov et al., 2013b) and SAT (Turney et al., 2003) for evaluation. Compared to BATS and Google, E-KAR, UNIT 2, UNIT 4, and SAT contain more abstract and complex analogies and thus more difficult for humans.“

"The study uses RoBERTaLarge as the backbone model, training it on 10,000 randomly sampled data points from ANALOGYKB in a multiple-choice QA format, and further fine-tunes it on various benchmarks. Baselines include pre-trained word embeddings, sentence embeddings, and language models, as well as knowledge-enhanced models like ERNIE and LUKE to control for relational knowledge. To demonstrate the importance of data filtering, an unfiltered 10,000-sample version of ANALOGYKB is also tested, with human evaluation showing that about 63% of these do not form valid analogies. Since most benchmarks (except E-KAR) lack training sets, models are fine-tuned on their small development sets."

Analogy Recognition Task:

“We adopt six analogy benchmarks… and evaluate on analogy recognition (multiple choice QA).” (p. 10)

Analogy Generation Task:

“We test models on 100 test data sampled from three challenging benchmarks… each generation is evaluated by three annotators with Fleiss’s κ = 0.93.” (p. 13)

Analogy Explanation Task:

“We ask GPT-4 to generate explanations… we test InstructGPT003 and ChatGPT on 100 data samples… with Fleiss’s κ = 0.97.” (p. 14, Figure 6)
column9:
Strengths:
Recognition:
"1) The performance of sentence embeddings is inferior to word embeddings. The rationale is that such word analogy is based on relational rather than semantic similarity between two sentences. Therefore, taking the difference between two word embeddings is a more reasonable yet still problematic approach for finding word analogies. 2) Incorporating entity knowledge cannot improve model performance on analogy recognition; 3) The training data without checking brings noise and even degrades model performance, further emphasizing the importance of high-quality data in ANALOGYKB. 4) Training models on ANALOGYKB can significant improve model's performance by a huge margin"

Massive scale and diversity:

“To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to construct an analogy KB (ANALOGYKB) with a million scale and diverse relational structures.” (p. 3)

Effective hybrid filtering (LLM + rules + human):

“Rule-based filtering technique [is] rather effective... few manual corrections were required.” (p. 8, Table 4)

Support for generalization via abstract meta-relations:

“The relation [CEO] and the relation [head of government]... can be induced into a relation: head of organization.” (p. 7, Table 1)

Weaknesses:
Limited relational complexity:

“This paper only considers analogies involving one or two relations… analogies may involve multiple entities and relations.” (p. 16, Limitations)

Domain restriction:

“ANALOGYKB is constructed using data from Wikidata and ConceptNet, which do not include analogies in other domains such as the scientific domain.” (p. 16)
column10:
Strengths:
Multiple diverse evaluation setups:

“We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate… analogy recognition and generation tasks…” (Abstract)

Human agreement measures (Fleiss’s κ > 0.86) indicate strong inter-rater reliability:

“The data is annotated by two annotators with Fleiss’s κ = 0.86.” (p. 9)

Ablation studies for method validation:

“We create ablated variants... to prove the necessity of filtering.” (p. 11)

Weaknesses:
Limited coverage of metaphoric analogies:

“ANALOGYKB contains few analogies related to metaphor and science… which are not common in the KGs.” (p. 16)

Bias from underlying KG distributions:
While not explicitly stated, reliance on Wikidata/ConceptNet means underrepresentation of niche or non-encyclopedic analogies.
column11:
Challenges in Generation:
Implicit analogies are hard to detect:

“Discovering analogies from KGs is not a trivial task… interesting and diverse analogies are implicit… with more complex relations.” (p. 3)

LLMs may return semantically similar but non-analogous pairs:

“InstructGPT003 struggles to filter out similar but wrong relations… which requires further filtering.” (p. 8)
column12:
Challenges in Evaluation:
Relational complexity is constrained:

“This paper only considers analogies involving one or two relations… Future research should address how to bridge this gap.” (p. 16)

Missing domain-specific analogies (e.g., metaphors):

“It would be challenging… to reason about an analogy such as Protein synthesis in a cell is like a factory assembly line.” (p. 16)

column5: Knowledge-Based Systems
column6: Proteus: Visuospatial analogy in problem-solving
column7:
Proteus is a computational system designed to model analogical problem-solving using only visuospatial knowledge. 
1.Representation: Problems are encoded as symbolic 2D line drawings called s-images, which capture visual elements, spatial relations, and transformations.
2.Five Main Subtasks:
Retrieval: Uses feature-vector matching to recall potential source cases and constraint satisfaction with backtracking for selecting the best match.
Mapping: Aligns visual elements (objects, spatial relations) between the target and source s-images, potentially generating multiple mappings.
Transfer: Transfers each transformation step from the source to the target; arguments of transformations may be adapted via literals, functions, or analogical components.
Evaluation: Compares the propositions of the generated solution with those of a predefined correct answer.
Storage: Stores new problem-solving procedures as new cases in memory.
4.New Subtask Identified:
"Dynamic mapping generation between the intermediate knowledge states in the source and the target, when a step in the transferred procedure creates a new object." 
This means Proteus must dynamically update mappings when new visual elements are introduced during transfer (e.g., decomposing one object into several).
5.Knowledge Representation:
A uniform language called Covlan is used to represent visual elements, qualitative variables (e.g., size, direction), and transformations (e.g., move, decompose, replicate), ensuring consistency across subtasks.
column9:
Strengths：
1.Unified Knowledge Representation:
Proteus uses a consistent visuospatial language (Covlan) across all analogy subtasks, promoting integration and coherence 
2.Comprehensive Subtask Coverage:
Unlike previous systems (e.g., ANALOGY, Letter Spirit), Proteus addresses all major analogy subtasks: retrieval, mapping, transfer, evaluation, and storage
3.Multi-step Procedure Transfer:
Proteus supports the analogical transfer of multi-step problem-solving procedures, not just isolated attributes or shapes 
4.Dynamic Intermediate Mapping:
It uniquely handles cases where transformations generate new objects during problem solving, requiring on-the-fly mapping between evolving states
Demonstrated on Classical Analogy Problems:
Proteus successfully solves canonical problems like the fortress–tumor scenario, demonstrating that visuospatial knowledge can support complex analogical reasoning in specific domains.
Weaknesses：
1.No Support for Causal or Functional Knowledge:
"The evaluation subtask appears to require (non-visuospatial) causal and functional knowledge..." 
Proteus cannot evaluate solutions using only visuospatial information and relies on handcrafted solution specifications.
2.Multiple Mappings Without Ranking:
Proteus generates several mappings based solely on structural constraints and lacks semantic or pragmatic filtering, which can lead to inefficiency and trial-and-error transfer 
3.Limited Generalization:
Its reliance on 2D visual representations makes it less suitable for domains that require abstract, symbolic, or functional representations beyond spatial structure.
Scalability Constraints in Retrieval:
Although retrieval is optimized using constraint satisfaction, efficiency may still degrade in very large case bases due to the complexity of visual graph matching

column5: Artificial Intelligence
column6: Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction
column7:
“Our direct concern in this paper is only with (1), retrieval of an analog in the absence of any external guidance as to what information in memory is relevant.” (Section 1
Constraints:
1.Semantic Similarity – similarity of predicates and concepts based on a semantic network.
2.Structural Consistency – preservation of relational structure between elements.
3.Pragmatic Centrality – preference for central or important propositions in the analog.
ARCS uses a semantic similarity scoring system that distinguishes between identity (1.0), synonymy (0.9), superordinate (0.8), and antonym (−0.5) relations
column8:
Evaluation method:
The authors evaluate their analogical retrieval system, ARCS (Analog Retrieval by Constraint Satisfaction), through simulation-based testing. They assess the system’s ability to retrieve relevant analogs from memory under multiple constraints using handcrafted analogical scenarios (e.g., the tumor/lightbulb problem) and compare the model’s performance to known results from psychological experiments on human analogy use.

Evaluation task used:
The main task is analogical retrieval: given a probe structure (e.g., a medical problem), the system must retrieve one or more stored analogs (e.g., a similar story or problem from memory) that best satisfy constraints on similarity and relevance. The system operates on predicate-calculus representations of structured knowledge across different domains (e.g., radiation problems, parables, plays).

What aspects of analogy are used to evaluate:
The evaluation focuses on three key aspects of analogical retrieval:

Semantic similarity – Do retrieved analogs contain concepts similar in meaning (e.g., dog ↔ cat)?

Structural consistency (isomorphism) – Do analogs share relational structure (e.g., bite(dog, boy) ↔ bite(cat, girl))?

Pragmatic centrality – Are retrieved analogs relevant to the current goal or purpose (e.g., solving a problem)?

These are tested via constraint satisfaction, where each analog is evaluated based on how well it fulfills all three constraints simultaneously.

What evaluation metric used:

Activation level of retrieval units: The core output is a quantitative activation score for each candidate analog in the connectionist network. The analog with the highest activation is selected as most relevant.

Qualitative comparison to human behavior: The authors validate the system’s performance against prior psychological studies (e.g., Holyoak & Koh, Ross) showing how humans prefer analogs with shared goals or relational structures.

Case analysis: Example-based correctness checks (e.g., correctly retrieving lightbulb analogy given a tumor problem).

No standard numerical metrics like accuracy or F1 are used—the model's behavior is compared qualitatively to known experimental results in cognitive science.

Is it automatic or manual:

The retrieval process is fully automatic, driven by parallel constraint satisfaction in a localist connectionist network.

The evaluation of output is manual, involving human interpretation of whether the retrieved analog matches expected outcomes based on psychological benchmarks.

Special terms explained:

ARCS (Analog Retrieval by Constraint Satisfaction): A computational model that retrieves analogs based on satisfying semantic, structural, and pragmatic constraints in parallel.

Semantic similarity: Defined via lexical relationships such as synonymy, kind-of (taxonomy), or part-whole.

Structural consistency (Isomorphism): A relational alignment between the source and target structures that preserves predicate-argument structure.

Pragmatic centrality: The importance of analogs for achieving the system’s current goal (e.g., problem-solving relevance).

Activation level: A scalar value representing how well a retrieved analog satisfies all constraints—higher means more relevant.
column9:
Strengths:
1.Constraint Integration:
ARCS goes beyond simple semantic matching by incorporating structure and pragmatics:
“Our model treats semantic similarity as the dominant constraint on retrieval, but not the only one.” (Section 2
2.Psychological Plausibility:
The model reproduces human-like retrieval preferences in classic analogical tasks (e.g., tumor-lightbulb problem, Ross statistics problem):
“The order of retrievability of the different types of analogs by ARCS... corresponds well with empirical psychological data.” (Section 6.1
3.Efficient Parallel Computation:
ARCS retrieves analogs in parallel without explicit search across all possible mappings:
“The algorithm has the advantage of simultaneously determining the best way to satisfy... all of the constraints.” (Section 5.1
Better Performance than Other Models:
Compared to ACT*, PI, and CYRUS, ARCS is more flexible, requires no pre-indexing, and achieves higher recall:
“ARCS has higher recall and precision than other retrieval systems that use only semantic similarity or pragmatics.” (Section 6.1

Weaknesses:
1..Semantic Similarity Dominates the Process:
Retrieval is only triggered for propositions that match semantically:
“ARCS does not compare the probe with every structure in the knowledge base, but considers only those that have semantically similar predicates.” (Section 5.1
2.Heuristic Parameter Values:
The semantic similarity weights (e.g., for synonyms, antonyms) are manually set:
“The specific values have no empirical justification.” (Section 5.2
3.Limited Scalability Due to Manual Knowledge Encoding:
Input analogs must be encoded as semantic networks, which constrains practical deployment:
“The knowledge base is still rather small. Also, its attribute set is very limited.” (Section 6.2
column10:
Strengths of Analogy Evaluation
Psychologically Grounded Validation
The model’s outputs are evaluated by comparing them to findings from cognitive psychology experiments, such as those by Holyoak & Koh and Ross. This gives the evaluation a strong cognitive plausibility and aligns model performance with human behavior.

Multidimensional Evaluation Criteria
The evaluation incorporates three major analogical constraints—semantic similarity, structural consistency, and pragmatic relevance—offering a richer and more realistic assessment of analogical quality than single-metric approaches.

Dynamic Activation-Based Scoring
Analogical matches are evaluated using continuous activation levels derived from constraint satisfaction, allowing the model to express graded similarity and relevance, rather than binary correct/incorrect judgments.

Demonstrated Usefulness Across Domains
The evaluation shows that the model retrieves context-appropriate analogs across diverse scenarios (e.g., radiation treatment, moral parables), supporting its generalizability and explanatory power.

Weaknesses of Analogy Evaluation
No Quantitative Performance Benchmarks
The evaluation lacks explicit accuracy metrics, precision, recall, or comparison scores. Instead, it relies on subjective interpretations of whether a retrieved analog “makes sense” given a probe.

Manual and Example-Based Validation
Outputs are assessed through manual inspection of a few illustrative cases, rather than through large-scale testing or statistically meaningful evaluations.

No Direct Human Judgment of Model Output
While human psychology is referenced, no empirical user studies were conducted to judge whether human participants agree with the model’s analogical matches or ranking decisions.

Limited Error Analysis
The paper does not systematically analyze when or why the model might fail to retrieve a valid analog—such as in cases of ambiguous goals, partial matches, or noisy input representations.

Evaluation Constrained to Synthetic Inputs
All tests are conducted on hand-encoded, structured symbolic representations; the evaluation does not test the model's robustness with naturalistic or automatically parsed inputs.
column11:
Limitations and Challenges in Generation
Manual Representation Construction
All analogs and target problems are represented in predicate-calculus form, which must be hand-crafted by experts. This limits scalability and prevents application to raw text or real-world data without significant preprocessing.

Reliance on Predefined Similarity and Centrality Relations
The system assumes access to predefined semantic networks and goal structures to assess similarity and pragmatic centrality. The authors note that this knowledge is non-trivial to build or generalize, and often context-dependent.

Constraint Interaction Complexity
Satisfying semantic, structural, and pragmatic constraints simultaneously can lead to trade-offs and complexity in determining the “best” analog. There is no global optimization framework to ensure the most balanced retrieval across all dimensions.

Limited Role of Learning
The ARCS system does not adapt its constraint weights or retrieval strategy based on experience. It lacks learning mechanisms that would allow it to improve its analogical inferences over time or across tasks.
column12:
Limitations and Challenges in Evaluation
Absence of Quantitative Performance Metrics
The evaluation does not involve numerical accuracy, recall, or precision. This makes it difficult to compare ARCS to other models or measure progress objectively.

No Large-Scale or Automated Testing
Evaluation is carried out through a small number of hand-designed examples, with no automated benchmark dataset or statistical evaluation.

Lack of Human Subject Experiments
While the model is inspired by psychological findings, it is not directly tested with human participants to assess whether its outputs are perceived as analogous or relevant by people.

No Systematic Error Analysis
The authors do not discuss when or why the model fails, nor do they offer strategies for handling ambiguous, noisy, or conflicting inputs—common in real-world analogical reasoning.

Constraint Prioritization Remains Unresolved
The paper acknowledges that no general rule exists for determining the relative importance of semantic, structural, and pragmatic constraints in different contexts. This remains an open challenge for both the model and its evaluation.

column5: IFAC Proceedings Volumes
column6: Formalisation of an Approximate Reasoning: The Analogical Reasoning
column7:
The paper presents a formal model of analogical reasoning implemented in the ARCHES system, based on the paradigm:
“A is to B what C is to D” — expressing “a resemblance of relationships,” where A and B belong to structure P, and C and D belong to structure T. (Section III
Core Mechanism:
The analogical inference derives D from known elements A, B, and C using structural similarity and dependency relations.
The similarity is formalized via =⇒-unification, a variant of logical unification adapted for approximate reasoning.
The inference rule is:
“A of P resembles C of T
BUT B derives from P
THEREFORE D derives from T.” (Section III
Structural Mapping:
Analogical reasoning in ARCHES is implemented as a mapping function f:
“The analogical model of ARCHES is defined as a particular mapping between two structures P and T… permitting the derivation of new knowledge from T by transferring a partial description from P to T.” (Section IV.2, p.139)
The mapping f transforms the descriptive structures from P to T only when:
B and D share the same structure (RB = RO)
A and C are sufficiently similar (RA ∩ RC ≠ ∅)
The dependency relations are satisfied, indicating that B depends on A and D on C.
“If f represents locally the identity function… then D is analogically inferred.” (Section IV.2
column8:
Evaluation method:
The evaluation of analogy in this paper is primarily theoretical and model-driven. Rather than applying empirical tasks or benchmarks, the authors assess analogical reasoning by analyzing its logical structure, failure cases, and applicability within the ARCHES symbolic system. The model is validated through formal examples and counterexamples that test whether the analogical inferences conform to specific predefined hypotheses about similarity, dependency, and inferential transfer.

Evaluation task used:
There is no standardized NLP or classification task. Instead, evaluation is carried out through case-based logical reasoning scenarios, such as whether a specific proposition (e.g., "the Moon is inhabited by men") can or cannot be analogically inferred from known facts (e.g., Earth is round and inhabited). These examples serve as conceptual test cases embedded within the model to examine inference validity under different structural and semantic conditions.

What aspects of analogy are used to evaluate:
The evaluation focuses on:

Structural similarity between sub-structures (A is to B as C is to D),

Information completeness (i.e., how much descriptive data is available),

Dependency relations between state properties,

Transferability of knowledge from one structure to another within the ARCHES system,

And consistency of analogical inferences with deductive reasoning when applicable.

The goal is to test whether the system can validly generate new knowledge from incomplete domains using analogy without contradicting established facts.

What evaluation metric used:
No quantitative metrics are used. Instead, the authors rely on:

Logical validity checks (can the conclusion be derived analogically but not deductively?),

Semantic plausibility of analogical inferences,

Failure case analysis (e.g., invalid analogies due to weak similarity or missing dependency relations).

These are framed through hypothesis-driven conditions, not numerical scores.

Is it automatic or manual:
The evaluation is manual and formal. All reasoning and assessment are based on formal logic, symbolic matching, and human-defined rules in the ARCHES system. The authors aim for future automation (e.g., PROLOG implementation), but the current paper’s evaluation is theoretical.

Special terms explained:

ARCHES: A symbolic system for knowledge representation and reasoning in the human sciences. It includes logic-based representations of concepts, individuals, and state relations.

=?-unification: A custom matching operation used in ARCHES to determine structural similarity and evaluate analogical mappings.

Dependency graph: A user-defined structure encoding conditions under which certain features (e.g., CLIMATE) depend on others (e.g., LOCATION), used to validate or invalidate analogical inferences.

Analogical model: A formal mapping function f that transfers descriptive elements between substructures, allowing analogical inference when structural and semantic conditions are met.
column9:
Strengths :
1.Formal logic-based model:
“The analogical inference rule defined… specifies this with the help of the four sub-structures A, B, C and D.” (Section III
2.Approximate reasoning in incomplete domains:
“This analogical inference provides conditional assertions whose logical validity is not postulated because it operates on incompletely described universes.” (Section III
3.Dependency constraints support plausible transfer:
“The dependency relation indicates the realization that B (respectively D) is conditioned by the existence of A (respectively C).” (Section III
4.Compatibility with humanistic domains:
“ARCHES is essentially used for applications concerning human sciences.” (Section II
5.Robust unification-based similarity assessment:
“Similarity is evaluated with the help of the =⇒-unification.” (Section V.2
Weaknesses :
1.No guarantee of logical validity:
“This analogical inference is manifestly non-valid… inference is based on the resemblance of two very incomplete descriptions…” (Section III
2.Heuristic dependency criteria must be externally provided:
“Dependency relations can be fixed by experts… Nonetheless, they can just as well be determined automatically.” (Section V.1
3.Similarity is necessary but not sufficient:
“If f never represents the identity function, then A and C are different and sub-structure D cannot be proved by analogy.” (Section IV.2
4.Sensitive to knowledge coverage:
“The limit of analogical reasoning in ARCHES is determined by two particular values: the identity… and the exhaustivity… thus it is therefore deductive reasoning.” (Section III
column10:
Strengths of Analogy Evaluation
Formal Logical Grounding
The evaluation of analogical reasoning is deeply rooted in formal logic, with carefully defined inference rules, constraints, and conditions, which provides a rigorous foundation for assessing when analogical conclusions are valid or not.

Explicit Hypothesis Framework
The evaluation is guided by a clear set of five foundational hypotheses about analogical reasoning (e.g., structural similarity, dependency, and completeness), allowing for a principled and explainable assessment of analogical inferences.

Use of Counterexamples
The authors use explicit invalid analogy cases (e.g., inferring that the Moon is inhabited like Earth) to demonstrate limitations and test the robustness of their formal model—this is a rare but effective technique for evaluating reasoning boundaries.

Model-based Validity Checking
Evaluation involves verifying consistency within a formal symbolic system (ARCHES), ensuring that analogical conclusions don’t contradict prior knowledge or exceed defined dependencies.

Weaknesses of Analogy Evaluation
No Empirical or Automated Testing
The evaluation is entirely theoretical, without empirical data, benchmarks, or automated testing on real-world tasks or corpora—limiting its scalability and practical validation.

No Quantitative Metrics
There are no numerical metrics (e.g., accuracy, precision) or standardized measures to assess analogy performance, making comparisons or reproducibility difficult.

Manually Defined Validity Conditions
All dependency graphs and logical assumptions are defined manually by experts, which may introduce subjectivity and limit transferability to new domains.

No Human Judgment or Task-based Validation
The system lacks human evaluation of analogy quality and does not tie evaluation to tasks like QA, generation, or classification, which could make it more useful in applied contexts.

Limited to Closed Symbolic Systems
Evaluation is confined to the closed universe of the ARCHES system, and the method’s effectiveness in open, noisy, or real-world environments remains untested.
column11:
Limitations and Challenges in Generation
Dependence on Incomplete Descriptions
Analogical reasoning is applied precisely when deductive reasoning fails—i.e., when the knowledge base is incompletely described. This makes the generated analogical inferences inherently uncertain and prone to invalid conclusions.

Risk of Invalid Analogical Inference
The authors provide examples where analogy produces false conclusions (e.g., inferring the Moon is inhabited like the Earth) due to weak or misleading structural similarity. This highlights the fragility of analogical reasoning in the absence of strong semantic or dependency links.

No Guarantee of Semantic Coherence
Analogical generation may connect facts with no meaningful dependency, as seen in the example where “shape” and “population” are unrelated, yet analogically inferred. This reflects a core limitation in semantic awareness during generation.

Manual Definition of Structures and Relations
All substructures, features, and dependency relations must be manually constructed within the ARCHES system, requiring extensive domain expertise and limiting scalability.

Unclear Heuristics for Similarity Thresholds
While similarity is central to analogical reasoning, the model provides no robust or dynamic method for determining how much similarity is “enough” to justify inference.
column12:
Limitations and Challenges in Evaluation
Lack of Empirical Validation
The analogical reasoning framework is not evaluated through data-driven experiments or real-world tasks. The model’s soundness is shown only via formal examples and logic-based discussion.

No Quantitative Metrics
The paper does not define any measurable evaluation criteria (e.g., accuracy, precision, utility), making it difficult to assess performance systematically or compare against other models.

No Human Judgment or Usability Study
The analogical outputs are not reviewed by human users or experts for interpretability, plausibility, or usefulness, so practical effectiveness remains untested.

Evaluation Confined to Synthetic Examples
All evaluations are performed on toy examples within a symbolic framework, and the system has not been deployed or evaluated in real-world domains such as law, medicine, or education (despite being motivated by them).

Ambiguity in Negative Criteria Handling
The model focuses primarily on positive similarity criteria, while the authors acknowledge that negating factors (e.g., lack of atmosphere) could be crucial for blocking invalid inferences—but their treatment is limited or heuristic.

column5: Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
column6: {A}na{DE}1.0: A Novel Data Set for Benchmarking Analogy Detection and Extraction
column7:
This paper does not focus on generating analogies but rather on detecting and extracting analogies from web documents. The task introduced is called AnaDE, which includes three subtasks:

“We propose and study a new task, called Analogy Detection and Extraction (AnaDE), which includes three synergistic sub-tasks: 1) detecting documents containing analogies, 2) extracting text segments that make up the analogy, and 3) identifying the source and target concepts being compared.” (Abstract)

The analogies were collected from Metamia.com, a crowdsourced site of user-submitted analogies, forming a dataset called AnaDE1.0.
column8:
The three sub-tasks were benchmarked using a mix of classical ML and transformer-based models:
1. AnaDet (Analogy Document Detection)
Framed as a binary classification task using full web pages.
Evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1.
Models used: BERT variants, Longformer, Random Forest, Logistic Regression.
“We frame the problem as a binary classification problem... and benchmark them on our task.” (Section 4.1)

2. AnaSE (Analogy Segment Extraction)
Framed as an extractive QA task (span selection).
Evaluated using Exact Match (EM) and F1 score.
“We frame the problem as an answer span extraction task.” (Section 4.2.1)

3. AnaConE (Analogy Concept Extraction)
Framed as token classification for extractive models.
Generative models prompted for source/target concepts.
Evaluated via alignment-based word-level EM and F1.
“We align each predicted concept to its best matching ground truth... and take an average over all aligned predicted concepts.” (Section 4.3.1)
column9:
Strengths:

The dataset includes long-form analogies with context.

Analogies cover broad domains like science, society, health, etc.

“About half of the analogies have ≥40 words... suggesting several analogies have detailed explanations.” (Section 3.2.1)

Weaknesses:

The dataset contains noisy or ambiguous samples.

Lack of control over analogy quality due to crowd-sourced submissions.

“The process of extracting and labeling analogies introduces the potential for accuracy errors... analogies can be subjective and open to interpretation.” (Section 6: Limitations)
column10:
Strengths:

Multiple transformer-based models were benchmarked systematically.

Longformer performs best due to handling longer contexts.

“Longformer model achieves the best performance on all the tasks... especially on tasks where the input is the full web page.” (Conclusion)

Weaknesses:

Annotation noise affects evaluation (e.g., analogies missed or labeled inconsistently).

Low generalizability in models for analogies without common markers.

“Although the dataset is not perfect... the noise in the negative set would unlikely favor any particular method.” (Section 3.2.2)

“Missing common analogy indicators... all the models failed.” (Section 4.2.4)
column11:
1. Data quality from Metamia is inconsistent:

“We discarded 5% of records due to issues such as no analogy or irrelevant texts... another 10.5% due to concept mismatch.” (Section 3.1.1)

**2. Challenge in collecting hard negatives for AnaDet:

“To make our dataset more useful... we retrieved ‘harder’ negative samples... using Bing search API.” (Section 3.1.2)

3. Analogies vary greatly in structure and length:

“We observe that about half of the analogies have ≥40 words or are longer than 2 sentences.” (Section 3.2.1)
column12:
1. Dataset contains annotation noise and inconsistencies:

“Multiple sub-analogies can be present... which should all be in the ground truth.” (Section 4.3.3)

2. Difficulty in establishing gold standards:

“It is also not immediately clear how we should evaluate it... we align each predicted concept to its best matching ground truth.” (Section 4.3.1)

3. Fine-grained classification requires longer context handling:

“Smaller models fine-tuned on our dataset perform better than the non-finetuned ChatGPT... further suggesting the value of our dataset.” (Conclusion)

column5: Proceedings of the 15th Conference on Creativity and Cognition
column6: Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies: Exploring Large Language Models’ Capacity for Augmenting Cross-Domain Analogical Creativity
column7:
The authors use prompt-based generation (with GPT-3, text-davinci-002) to generate cross-domain analogies from structured problem descriptions in design tasks.
“We crafted a structured natural-language instruction prompt for generating cross-domain analogies... and used these prompts to generate 480 cross-domain analogies across six design problems.” (Section 1)

Prompts specified four components: stakeholder, context, goal, obstacle.
“Dividing a design problem into four components—stakeholder, context, goal and obstacle—led to higher quality outputs.” (Section 3.1)

They tested zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting.
“We used GPT-3 to generate 20 analogies each for input problems, for each of three prompt programming paradigms: zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot.” (Section 3.1)
column8:
They used human ratings to evaluate both general and contextual usefulness of generated analogies.

Prompt Engineering Evaluation:
480 analogies rated by a PhD researcher for potential usefulness, semantic similarity, and duplication.

“Analogies were rated for potential usefulness for creative reformulation... whether it was unique... and whether it could inspire new formulations.” (Section 3.2)

Creative Task Evaluation (Study 1):
110 participants each reformulated a design problem with two analogies.

Rated analogies for helpfulness (1–5 scale).

Also evaluated behavioral indicators (problem reformulation through adding or rejecting components).

“The median rated helpfulness of analogies was 4 out of 5.” (Section 4.2.1)
column9:
Strengths:

High rate of judged usefulness:

“70% of outputs were both unique and judged... potentially useful.” (Abstract)

Human ratings confirmed analogies spurred new thinking:

“Analogies were rated as helpful... primarily spurring new considerations... shifts in perspectives... redefining key elements.” (Abstract)

Weaknesses:

Shallow or redundant analogies still occurred:

“Examples of duplicate analogies... with substantial verbatim overlap.” (Figure 4)

Lack of deeper domain-specific insight:

“Many of the analogies seemed quite diverse, but didn’t describe deep details about any particular domain.” (Section 6.2.2)
column10:
Strengths:

Task-embedded human evaluation captured real usage.

Combined quantitative metrics (ratings, coding) and qualitative insights.

“Participants rated the analogies overall as helpful... and described the analogies as augmenting/broadening their thinking process.” (Section 6.1)

Weaknesses:

No correlation between heuristic a priori usefulness and actual usefulness during task:

“No statistically significant correlation between a priori usable ratings and in-use helpfulness ratings.” (Section 4.2.3)

Limited inter-rater agreement in early stages of annotation:

“This resulted in low inter-rater reliability... we refined the coding scheme.” (Section 4.1.4)
column11:
1. Prompt engineering complexity:

“Iterative process... evaluating response from an LLM.” (Section 3.1)

2. Duplication and overfitting in one-shot/few-shot paradigms:

“Some duplicate analogies shared very similar concepts... with substantial verbatim overlap.” (Figure 4)

**3. Generating deep insights remains difficult:

“It is unclear to what extent these analogies could spark deep insights... may reflect limitations in domain knowledge.” (Section 6.2.2)
column12:
1. Context-sensitive usefulness hard to predict:

“Lack of correlation between pre-judged potential usefulness and helpfulness in the context.” (Section 4.2.3)

2. Risk of harmful outputs:

“Upper bound of ∼25% of outputs as potentially harmful... mostly due to upsetting content.” (Section 5.2)

3. Limited generalizability of human screening:

“We make no claims as to their generality to other contexts.” (Section 5.1)

column5: Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2023
column6: CAM: A Large Language Model-based Creative Analogy Mining Framework
column7:
The CAM framework generates analogies using prompted large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-3, following a three-stage generate-evaluate-refine pipeline:

“The framework consists of the following three main steps: (1) Generate analogies using PLMs with effectively designed prompts, (2) Evaluate their quality using scoring functions, and (3) Refine the low-quality analogies by another round of prompt-based generation.” (Section 4)

The input is a target concept (e.g., “candidate generation”), and the model is prompted to produce an analogy involving a source concept and an explanation of the mapping.

“The analogy mining problem is to identify a source concept expressed as a phrase that is analogous... and provides an explanation... on how the two concepts are connected.” (Section 3)
column8:
CAM evaluates analogies using three criteria: analogical style, meaningfulness, and novelty.

Analogical Style Scorer: Classifies whether a generated text is analogy-like.

Meaningfulness Scorer: Measures self-agreement across different model configurations.

Novelty Scorer: Uses semantic distance from known web analogies.

“We design scoring functions to assess the responses generated... in terms of the analogical style, meaningfulness, and novelty.” (Section 4)

Evaluation was performed using crowd-sourced human ratings on Likert scales and validated against expert evaluations:

“Overall, 13.7%... were highly creative analogies. Using a lower threshold, 56.37%... were at least somewhat creative.” (Section 5.3.3)

Also, automatic scorers were evaluated using Kendall’s Tau and NDCG@k to assess correlation with human ratings.
column9:
Strengths:

Effective at generating analogies in zero-shot settings.

Capable of mining creative analogies, not just surface-level paraphrases.

“CAM... can mine 13.7% highly-creative and 56.37% somewhat-creative analogies.” (Abstract)

“PLMs can be used as a powerful creativity mining tool... opening up a novel paradigm.” (Conclusion)

Weaknesses:

Output quality highly depends on prompt design and domain.

Some analogies are trivial or uninformative in technical domains.

“Some rare, technical concepts in the ML and Cybersecurity domain... represent the model’s ‘best guess’.” (Section 5.4.2)
column10:
Strengths:

Multi-faceted evaluation using style, meaning, and novelty.

Scorers can be used unsupervised or fine-tuned with human feedback.

“Our results show that the supervised models are generally better... confirming that supervision is helpful.” (Section 5.4.2)

Weaknesses:

Evaluation is subjective, with low inter-annotator agreement:

“Krippendorf’s α for Meaningfulness: ML = 0.136... Novelty: ML = 0.197” (Section 5.3.2)

Semantic novelty scoring is difficult in domains with low online data:

“Science domain seems to be the most challenging as no method was able to beat the random baseline.” (Section 5.4.3)
column11:
Creative prompt design without direct examples is difficult:

“By design, these prompts do not explicitly instruct the model to generate creative analogies.” (Section 5.1.1)

Low recall without iterative refinement:

“We found that majority (86.8%)... were classified as being analogy-like after refinement.” (Section 5.5)

Domain sensitivity: Some domains (e.g., cybersecurity) have fewer analogy-rich training examples.
column12:
Subjectivity and expertise gap among crowd workers:

“Relatively low inter-annotator agreement... another possibility could be that the crowd workers were not experts.” (Section 5.3.2)

Lack of ground-truth analogies for comparison:

“Evaluation of creative analogies also poses special challenges since we cannot possibly enumerate all the creative analogies in advance.” (Section 3)

Trade-off between novelty and meaning:

“Completely random text would be highly novel but not meaningful... their combination could be optimized based on the application.” (Section 4)

column5: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2023
column6: An Analogical Reasoning Method Based on Multi-task Learning with Relational Clustering
column7:
“We proposed a multi-task learning method for analogical QA task… The first task aims to train an analogical classifier by supervised learning. The second task is an auxiliary task based on relation clustering…” (Section 2)
Method Components:
Word-Pair Representations:
Word pairs (e.g., "fruit: apple") are input as “[CLS] word1 [MASK] word2”. The embedding at the [MASK] token is used to represent the relational vector:
“We obtain word-pair representations by using embeddings of [MASK] tokens so that we can effectively use the explicit knowledge learned during pretraining.” (Section 2.1)
Analogical Classification:
The fused vector of the query pair and candidate pair is used as input to a classifier:
“We fuse the representations of query and each candidate… to determine whether they are analogous or not.” (Section 2.2)
Unsupervised Relational Clustering:
K-means clustering is applied to word-pair representations to generate pseudo-labels for relation classification:
“We group the features with k-means algorithm… and generate pseudo-labels… [used] as supervised signals to update the weights of the network.” (Section 2.3)
Multi-task Learning:
Combines losses from the analogical classification and the relation clustering to jointly train the model:
“The total loss… is the weighted sum of the losses of the two tasks.” (Section 2.4)
column8:
Evaluation method:
The authors evaluate their method through experimental benchmarking on four public analogical QA datasets. The performance is measured by comparing model accuracy against a range of baselines including word embedding methods, relation classification methods, and prompt-based language model approaches. The evaluation also includes ablation studies to test the contribution of each component in their model.

Evaluation task used:
The main evaluation task is a multiple-choice analogical QA task: given a query word pair and several candidate word pairs, the model must select the most analogous candidate. This task tests whether the model can recognize relational similarity between word pairs, rather than just attributional similarity.

What aspects of analogy are used to evaluate:
The evaluation focuses on assessing:

The model’s ability to recognize relational similarity (not just surface similarity) between word pairs.

The effectiveness of unsupervised relation clustering in improving word-pair representation for analogy tasks.

The robustness of the system across different domains and difficulty levels, including the challenging E-KAR dataset.

What evaluation metric used:

Accuracy is the primary metric used across all datasets to measure whether the correct analogical pair was selected.

Ablation accuracy comparison is used to evaluate the effect of each component (e.g., removing the clustering task or [MASK] tokens).

Case studies are used for qualitative analysis, showing how the model avoids being misled by attributional similarity.

Is it automatic or manual:

The evaluation process is fully automatic: predictions are scored using accuracy against ground truth labels.

Manual interpretation is included in the case study section for explanatory purposes but is not a core part of the evaluation pipeline.

Special terms explained:

Analogical QA task: A multiple-choice format where the goal is to identify the most analogous word pair to a given query.

Relation clustering: An auxiliary task using k-means to assign pseudo-labels to word-pair representations, helping improve relational understanding without manual labels.

[MASK] token: A token in pre-trained language models used to help the model focus on relations by masking contextual words.

Multi-task learning: Training jointly on the main analogical QA task and an auxiliary relation classification task to improve generalization and relational reasoning.
column9:
Strengths:
1.Explicit focus on relational similarity:
“Our method guides the model to analyze the relation similarity in analogical reasoning without relation labels.” 
2.Unsupervised auxiliary constraint improves generalization:
“The auxiliary task is helpful for analogical QA task… multi-task learning can promote [MASK] tokens to obtain more knowledge from the PLMs.” (Section 3.5)
3.Avoids surface-level attributional traps:
“Our method performs well in prediction even when the query and candidate… have high degree of both attributional similarity and relationship similarity.” (Section 3.5, Case Study)
4.End-to-end architecture with no reliance on external corpora:
“We avoid the noise introduced by external corpora and the problem of obtaining a representation of word pairs that do not co-occur in the corpus.” (Section 3.4)
Weaknesses:
1.Relies on pseudo-labels instead of gold-standard relation labels:
“Pseudo-labels is not a relation label for ground-truth because we don’t know the real relation of word pair.” (Section 2.3)
2.Unsupervised constraints are limited:
“The unsupervised constraints are limited… although wikidata can be used to create data for analogy classification, this requires much manual effort.” (Conclusion)
column10:
Strengths of Analogy Evaluation
Benchmark-Based Evaluation Across Multiple Datasets
The model is evaluated on four standard analogical reasoning datasets (E-KAR, SAT, Google, BATS), allowing robust and comparative assessment across a range of difficulty levels and linguistic domains.

Quantitative Accuracy Metrics
The evaluation uses accuracy as a clear, interpretable metric, which facilitates straightforward comparison with prior work and supports reproducibility.

Ablation Study Validates Model Components
The authors conduct controlled ablation experiments to isolate the effect of relational clustering and input design (e.g., the use of [MASK] tokens), showing the contribution of each design choice to analogical performance.

Qualitative Case Analysis
The paper provides case studies that illustrate how the model correctly identifies analogies while avoiding distractions from attributional similarity—offering insight into the model’s relational reasoning behavior.

Demonstrated Improvement on a Hard Dataset (E-KAR)
The model shows a notable performance gain on E-KAR, a particularly challenging analogical QA dataset, demonstrating the evaluation’s ability to reflect meaningful progress in analogical reasoning capabilities.

Weaknesses of Analogy Evaluation
Single-Metric Focus (Accuracy Only)
Evaluation relies solely on accuracy, with no exploration of fine-grained metrics like precision, recall, or reasoning trace quality—limiting depth of insight into the model’s analogical reasoning process.

No Human Judgment or Error Analysis
The paper does not include human evaluation of whether model outputs are genuinely analogous, nor does it provide systematic error analysis to examine failure cases or explain why certain errors occur.

No Direct Evaluation of Relation Clustering Quality
Although relational clustering is a central component of the model, its intrinsic quality (e.g., cluster coherence, purity) is not directly evaluated—only its downstream effect on QA performance is observed.

Limited Task Diversity
The evaluation is focused entirely on multiple-choice QA tasks. Other forms of analogical reasoning—such as mapping, explanation generation, or analogical inference—are not tested, reducing the breadth of evaluation.

Pseudo-label Uncertainty Not Quantified
Since the auxiliary task uses unsupervised pseudo-labels, it may introduce noise, but the evaluation does not quantify the reliability of these labels or their potential side effects.
column11:
Limitations and Challenges in Generation
Lack of Explicit Relation Labels
The analogical QA datasets used (e.g., E-KAR) do not contain gold relation labels, making it difficult to directly supervise relational learning. To overcome this, the model uses unsupervised clustering to create pseudo-labels, which may introduce noise.

Dependency on Pseudo-Labels from Clustering
Since the auxiliary relation classification task is based on k-means clustering, the quality of supervision is inherently limited by the quality of the clusters, which may not align with meaningful relational distinctions.

Attributional Similarity Interference
The authors acknowledge that models often confuse attributional similarity (e.g., synonyms) with relational analogy. This makes the analogy generation process vulnerable to misleading surface features if no constraints are applied.

Manual Prompt Sensitivity in Baselines
The paper notes that prior prompt-based methods (e.g., AutoPrompt) are sensitive to template wording and may extract noisy or irrelevant relational signals. Although their model avoids this, it suggests a broader challenge in prompting analogical reasoning.

No Ground-Truth for Auxiliary Task
The auxiliary relation classification task does not have true supervision, and performance relies on how well the clustering aligns with actual relational structures—an assumption that may not hold in complex cases.
column12:
Limitations and Challenges in Evaluation
Evaluation Based Solely on Accuracy
The authors only use accuracy as the evaluation metric for analogical QA. This provides a coarse view of performance and doesn’t assess why the model made certain analogical matches or whether its reasoning was sound.

Lack of Human Evaluation or Error Analysis
There is no manual review or human judgment on model outputs to validate if the chosen analogies are genuinely plausible. The absence of detailed error analysis also limits understanding of model failures.

Limited Task Scope
The model is only evaluated on multiple-choice analogy tasks. It is not tested on tasks involving explanation, inference, or analogy generation, which would more fully validate analogical understanding.

No Direct Measure of Relation Clustering Effectiveness
The unsupervised clustering used in the auxiliary task is not directly evaluated (e.g., cluster quality metrics), so it is unclear how much it contributes to actual relational reasoning performance.

Potential Overfitting to Benchmark Datasets
The paper reports improved performance on known datasets, but generalizability to other forms of analogy or open-domain reasoning is not tested.

column5: Proceedings of the 38th Annual Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences
column6: Analogy, Deduction and Learning
column7:
In the body of the paper, the authors primarily use an automatic analogy generation method based on a generalized symbolic machine learning framework. This framework builds on and extends the well-known Structure Mapping Engine (SME), which identifies analogies by aligning structurally similar relations between a known base (B) and a less known target (T). While SME is structurally grounded, the authors broaden its scope by incorporating a multi-strategy learning model that allows different types of analogical similarity—such as relational, causal, and semantic—to be learned. In their approach, analogies are generated by learning mappings between objects in B and T, using only positive examples (i.e., no counterexamples) drawn from First-Order Logic (FOL) descriptions. These descriptions are manually translated into SUO-KIF, a formal logic representation adapted for ontological reasoning.

The output of analogy generation is a set of new hypotheses—also expressed in SUO-KIF FOL—generated by applying the learned mappings to unmatched or matched portions of the base data. These hypotheses take the form of logical assertions, such as potential transfers of nuclear technology between countries, and are designed to be both interpretable and verifiable. Once generated, the hypotheses are automatically filtered using ontology-based deduction. This is done with the Sigma environment and its built-in Vampire theorem prover, which tests each hypothesis against a knowledge base composed of upper-level and domain-specific ontologies (e.g., SUMO, MILO, and WMD-related domains). The deduction phase discards hypotheses that are logically inconsistent or redundant, ensuring that the final output is both plausible and informative.

While the analogy generation and validation processes are largely automated, the conversion of unstructured text (e.g., country reports) into logic remains manual in the current setup. However, the authors aim to automate this step in the future by incorporating ontology-guided information extraction tools. Overall, the analogy generation is automatic, the data preparation is manual, and the deduction-based validation is automatic. The generated analogies are formal, logic-based hypotheses intended to support human analysts by suggesting novel, unbiased insights grounded in structured reasoning.
column8:
Evaluation Method Used by the Authors
Evaluation Approach:
The authors evaluate analogy generation indirectly through deductive validation rather than traditional benchmark tasks. After generating analogical hypotheses automatically, each hypothesis is tested against a large knowledge base (KB) using a first-order logic theorem prover (Vampire via the Sigma environment).

Task Used for Evaluation
Task Type:
Hypothesis validation task using knowledge bases—each hypothesis is checked to determine whether it is:

Redundant (already entailed by the KB),

Contradictory (logically refuted by the KB), or

Novel and plausible (not derivable but consistent with known facts).

This task simulates a real-world use case, where analogies are used to generate knowledge hypotheses (e.g., WMD collaborations between countries) that an intelligence analyst might investigate.

Aspect of Analogy Being Evaluated
What is being evaluated:

Usefulness and soundness of analogical hypotheses: whether they are logically valid, novel, and relevant for knowledge discovery.

Filtering effectiveness: how well the combined analogy + deduction system avoids false or nonsensical analogies.

Evaluation Metrics
Metrics Used:

Quantitative counts of hypotheses generated vs. those validated (i.e., passed logical checks). Example: 76 generated, 46 validated.

False positive / false negative rates, based on manual review of a subset of hypotheses.

No precision/recall or BLEU-like metrics are used; instead, the evaluation is centered on logical consistency and novelty within the KB.

Automatic or Manual Evaluation
Combination of both:

Automatic: Most of the evaluation is automated through logical deduction using Vampire.

Manual: Some hypotheses are manually reviewed to assess the false positive and false negative rates of the deductive validation.

Special Terms Explained
Vampire: A first-order logic theorem prover that automatically proves or disproves logical statements.

SUO-KIF: A logic-based representation language used to encode hypotheses and domain knowledge.

Hypothesis validation: A logical process that checks whether a generated analogy is valid by testing it against background knowledge.
column9:
Strengths of the Analogy Generation Method
Combines Analogy with Deduction:
A major strength is the two-stage approach—analogy generation followed by logical deduction—which helps filter out false or absurd analogies that many systems would otherwise retain.

Generalized, Symbolic Framework:
The system extends beyond traditional SME by allowing multi-strategy learning, enabling analogies based on not only structural similarity but also causal, semantic, or ontological similarities.

Formal Logical Representation (SUO-KIF):
Using first-order logic (FOL) ensures that generated analogies can be interpreted, reasoned with, and validated, making the output useful for real-world analytical reasoning (e.g., intelligence analysis).

Scalability with Ontologies:
The use of upper-level (SUMO), mid-level (MILO), and domain-specific ontologies enhances the interpretability and validation capacity of generated hypotheses, offering semantic richness.

Real-world Applicability:
The system produces unbiased, interpretable, and novel hypotheses in domains like WMD intelligence, showing practical relevance.

Weaknesses or Limitations
Manual Data Preprocessing:
The analogizer requires manual translation of unstructured text (e.g., intelligence reports) into logic form (SUO-KIF), which is labor-intensive and not scalable.

No Semantic Matching in Analogy Learning:
The analogy generator (based on SME) does not match semantically related predicates (e.g., "eat" vs. "consume") due to reliance on structural identity, leading to missed intelligent analogies.

Mixed Objects in Hypotheses:
Generated analogies can include “mixed” object sets (from both base and target) due to incomplete mappings, sometimes producing implausible or incoherent hypotheses.

High Dependence on Knowledge Base Coverage:
The quality of analogy evaluation is limited by how complete and accurate the KB is. Gaps in the KB lead to false negatives, i.e., discarding plausible hypotheses because they cannot be verified.

Limited Human Judgement Integration:
While the tool aims to aid human analysts, it does not incorporate human feedback during analogy generation itself (only during optional manual review), which limits adaptive refinement.
column10:
Strengths of the Analogy Evaluation Approach
Logical Rigor through Deductive Reasoning:
The use of first-order logic theorem proving (Vampire) provides a precise, formal basis for evaluating hypotheses. This enables clear identification of contradictions, redundancies, and logically novel outputs.

Semantic Awareness via Ontologies:
Evaluation is enhanced by incorporating SUMO, MILO, and domain-specific ontologies. These allow type checking, disjoint class validation, and commonsense reasoning, strengthening evaluation reliability.

Automatic and Scalable Filtering:
Once hypotheses are generated in logic form, automated evaluation can be run at scale without human intervention, supporting large-scale hypothesis testing across multiple entity pairs.

Practical Value for Analysts:
The evaluation mechanism helps prioritize novel and meaningful analogies for human review, making it highly applicable to real-world domains like intelligence or policy analysis.

Weaknesses or Limitations
Incomplete Knowledge Base Leads to False Negatives:
The biggest limitation is coverage gaps in the validation knowledge base (KB). Many plausible analogies are wrongly rejected simply because the KB lacks supporting or neutral facts—leading to false negatives.

Limited Evaluation Dimensions:
The system does not measure creativity, relevance, or usefulness of analogies from a human perspective. It focuses only on logical consistency, omitting subjective or task-specific utility assessments.

No Ground Truth or Human Ratings:
The evaluation lacks benchmark datasets or human-annotated gold standards. There is no precision/recall or accuracy metric, making it hard to compare with other analogy systems.

Manual Review is Sparse and Incomplete:
While some hypotheses were manually inspected, the process was not comprehensive, and the authors acknowledged that statistics on error rates (false positives/negatives) were incomplete at submission time.

Binary Pass/Fail Output:
The system treats hypotheses as either valid or invalid, without ranking or scoring their plausibility or novelty, which may limit granularity in downstream use.
column11:
Limitations and Challenges in Analogy Generation
Manual Data Translation

Input data (e.g., CNS summaries) must be manually translated into SUO-KIF, a formal logic language.

This process is labor-intensive, error-prone, and not scalable for large datasets.

Inflexible Structural Matching

The analogizer (based on SME) relies on exact predicate matching for analogies.

It misses semantically similar but syntactically different relations (e.g., “eat” vs. “consume”).

Incoherent Mixed Hypotheses

Generated hypotheses can contain objects from both base and target domains if mappings are incomplete.

This leads to implausible or confusing analogies, unless filtered.

No Use of Ontology During Analogy Generation

Ontological knowledge is only used during evaluation, not during generation.

This limits the ability to generate semantically richer or better-aligned hypotheses.

Single-Strategy Learning Limitation (in early version)

The earlier analogizer approximated SME and stopped at the first valid mapping.

Although improved later, this initially led to incomplete hypothesis coverage.
column12:
Limitations and Challenges in Analogy Evaluation
Knowledge Base Coverage Gaps

Evaluation relies on ontological and factual knowledge in the KB.

If the KB lacks domain-specific facts, valid hypotheses may be falsely rejected (false negatives).

No Human Judgment in Evaluation

The evaluation is fully logic-based, without human relevance, novelty, or creativity assessments.

Thus, hypotheses might be logically valid but not interesting or useful.

Binary Outcome Without Ranking

Hypotheses are accepted or discarded with no confidence score or ranking.

This limits flexibility in prioritizing or comparing outputs.

Limited Manual Review

Manual inspection of results was not exhaustive; statistics on false positives/negatives were incomplete at submission.

This leaves gaps in empirical evaluation quality.

Ontology Maintenance Challenge

The validation KB must be constantly updated to reflect new events and knowledge.

Authors note that this incremental knowledge growth is crucial but challenging to automate.

column5: Proceedings of the 30th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
column6: Know Your Needs Better: Towards Structured Understanding of Marketer Demands with Analogical Reasoning Augmented LLMs
column7:
In this paper, the authors propose a hybrid analogy-based generation framework called ARALLM (Analogical Reasoning Augmented Large Language Model) to transform natural language marketer demands into structured logical expressions in a formal language named SELL (Structured and Editable Logical Language). The generation method is centered around the idea that similar marketer demands tend to share similar reasoning steps and logical structures.
